newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope to receive Taiwanese in controversial meeting.
newsitem.headline: Pope to receive Taiwanese in controversial meeting.

text.p: In a move which could upset communist China, the Vatican said on Thursday that Pope John Paul will meet Taiwan's Vice-President Lien Chan next week.
Lien Chan will be the highest ranking Taiwanese official to visit the Vatican and meet the Pope, according to Raymond Tai, Taiwan's ambassador to the Vatican.
The Vatican said Lien had asked for the audience, which will take place next Tuesday when he stops in Rome on his way back from a visit to Nicaragua.
The Vatican is one of only 30 states that recognise the Republic of China government which retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after its civil war defeat by the communists.

The Vatican has no diplomatic ties with Beijing, which has often insisted that if the Holy See wants improved ties it must first break links with Taiwan. Beijing regards the island as a renegade province ineligible for sovereign recognition.

Beijing, which does not allow its Catholics to recognise the Pope's authority, wants the Vatican to recognise it as the sole legal government of China and has been critical of Church relations with Taiwan in the past.

A month ago Beijing responded to an appeal from the Pope to legalise the Roman Catholic Church, saying it wanted better relations with the Vatican but would brook no interference in China's internal affairs.
Ambassador Tai told Reuters he could not predict what Beijing's reaction to the visit would be but added: "They are not qualified to criticise an independent state like the Vatican.
"They (Beijing) should not interfere with the sovereign affairs of a state," Tai said.

The ambassador said Lien wanted to visit the Pope to express his support for the Pontiff's latest world day of peace message, which appealed to nations and groups to forgive past injuries in order to facilitate peace.
Recently Beijing has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.
After South Africa announced in November it would switch allegiance from Taipei to Beijing this year, senior Taiwanese officials have embarked on a series of damage-control visits overseas.
Lien and Foreign Minister John Chang have visited Ukraine, Singapore, Malaysia, Belgium, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan in the past year, seeking to firm up unofficial ties.
